extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in media, journalism, and the history/format of Time magazine
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of Time (magazine) covering its history, style, sections, special editions, design choices, circulation, and notable editorial practices. Useful for understanding how the magazine has defined and applied editorial and design conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timestyle / Writing style
rubrics_metrics.description: Time initially possessed a distinctively "acerbic, irreverent style", largely created by Hadden and sometimes called "Timestyle"; Timestyle made regular use of inverted sentences and popularized many neologisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and commentary in the article: the famous parody "Backward ran sentences until reeled the mind..."; Time coined or popularized words such as "socialite", "guesstimate", "televangelist", "pundit", and "tycoon"; it also used the "false title" construction sometimes called a "Time-style adjective."

rubrics_metrics.name: People‑focused cover editorial approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Time set out to tell the news through people; until the late 1960s the magazine's cover depicted a single person. More recently Time has incorporated "People of the Year" issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for cover selection: prioritize human-centered storytelling on the cover (single-person portraits historically), and dedicate special issues to groups or concepts (e.g., Person/People of the Year). The first issue featured Joseph G. Cannon as an example of single-person cover practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Red border as iconic cover identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Time is known for the red border on its cover, introduced in 1927; the border is an iconic design element and has only been changed a small number of times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the border is changed it signals a special issue or theme: e.g., black border for mourning after 9/11, green for Earth Day (2008), metallic silver for anniversaries, silver for the 'Most Influential Photos' and Queen Elizabeth II issues, and inclusion of names on the June 15, 2020 George Floyd cover. Use of border variations is an editorial/design signal reserved for notable occasions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person of the Year selection principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Person of the Year recognizes the individual or group of individuals who have had the biggest impact on news headlines over the past 12 months; the distinction is supposed to go to the person who, "for good or ill", has most affected the course of the year — it is not necessarily an honor or a reward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection rationale emphasizes impact rather than merit. Historical examples cited include Adolf Hitler and Joseph Stalin as Man(s) of the Year, 2006's unconventional selection "You", and 2017's "Silence Breakers"; editors have defended controversial choices by pointing to the 'for good or ill' criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time 100 selection principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Time assembles an annual list of the 100 most influential people of the year (originally the 100 most influential people of the 20th century).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format guidance: the issue typically fills the front cover with pictures from the list and devotes substantial space inside to individual write-ups; the list can exceed 100 entries when people are paired or share a spot.

rubrics_metrics.name: X cover usage protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: On rare occasions Time releases a special issue with a cover showing an X scrawled over the face of a man, a year, or a national symbol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical usage indicates the X cover marks definitive events such as death or defeat (e.g., Hitler after his death 1945; Japan flag after surrender 1945; Saddam Hussein 2003; Abu Musab al-Zarqawi 2006; Osama bin Laden 2011), or to mark a symbolic repudiation (e.g., crossing out the year '2020' and calling it 'the worst year ever'); use is exceptional and reserved for major, often terminal events or symbolic editorial statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Milestones section format
rubrics_metrics.description: Milestones is a section about significant events in the lives of famous people (births, marriages, divorces, deaths); until 1967 entries were short and formulaic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical older-format entry structure: terse label (e.g., "Died."), name and age, concise list of claims to fame, and a brief description of circumstances and place. The article gives a 1956 example and notes that the style was parodied for its formulaic nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listings section editorial standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Time historically had a weekly "Listings" section with capsule summaries or reviews of current significant films, plays, musicals, television programs, and literary bestsellers (similar to The New Yorker's 'Current Events').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Listings functioned as compact critical/contextual capsules for cultural items; the practice continued until the mid-1970s according to the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2007 redesign editorial and design principles
rubrics_metrics.description: In 2007 Time redesigned the magazine to update and modernize the format, implementing specific design and editorial changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documented changes include: reduced the red cover border to promote featured stories, enlarged column titles, reduced the number of featured stories, increased white space around articles, and accompanied opinion pieces with photographs of the writers. The redesign aimed to modernize visual hierarchy and readability; reactions included both criticism and praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time for Kids editorial format and audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Time for Kids is a division magazine of Time specially published for children and mainly distributed in classrooms; it contains some national news, a 'Cartoon of the Week', and a variety of popular-culture articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format constraints: the publication rarely exceeds ten pages front and back; it includes an annual environment issue timed near the end of the U.S. school term. Content and tone are adjusted for classroom/child audience and curricular distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time LightBox photography editorial focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Time LightBox is a photography blog created and curated by the magazine's photo department that explores contemporary photography from the perspective of the photo editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial emphasis is on more than photojournalism — covering documentary and fine art photography; it was recognized by awards (Life.com's 2011 Photo Blog Awards) and praised as an essential destination for those who appreciate contemporary photography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming and terminology influence as editorial practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Time introduced or popularized terminology (for example, the magazine introduced the names 'World War I' and 'World War II' in 1939), and popularized numerous neologisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reflects an editorial practice of coining or standardizing terms that can shape public discourse; the article cites examples of successful neologisms and some less successful ones (e.g., 'cinemactress'). The 'false title' construction and its labeling as a 'Time-style adjective' are noted as characteristic linguistic practices.
